summary: Opening a month-long Kartika parikrama, Indradyumna Swami frames the pilgrims as students on their first day of transcendental school, quoting a Braj-bhasa saying that in the classroom of Sri Vrindavan Dham love is the teacher, Radha and Krishna are the students, and the attentive gopis are their classmates, all learning to relish Krishna's pastimes. He glorifies Vrindavan as the best place in all creation and Kartika as the best time to learn about the Divine Couple and to serve them with pure devotion (amala-bhakti), showing through Srila Prabhupada's example and purports (such as Srimad-Bhagavatam 4.29.39-40) that the dham is supremely merciful—an expansion of Lord Balarama—and awakens love of God even in the sinful, so much so that Prabhupada invited the whole world, and elderly people especially, to settle there permanently and become brajabasis. The heart of the lecture answers how one truly 'enters' Vrindavan: citing Krishna Book chapter 38, he stresses that one cannot reach Vrindavan merely by buying a plane or train ticket or by being physically present, but must follow the ideal footsteps of Akrura. Retelling how Kamsa, having failed with daily demons because Krishna is Ajita (unconquerable), sent Akrura to lure Krishna and Balarama to Mathura to be killed by the wrestlers Chanura and Mustika, the Swami shows that Akrura was secretly a great devotee (gupta, hidden) who had to conceal his ecstasy and who approached the dham feeling himself a wretched, unqualified materialist—teaching that humility is the first qualification for entering Vraj, and that if we lack it we should at least 'desire to desire' it. He reinforces this with the humility of Prahlada Maharaj before Lord Nrisimhadev, of Krishnadas Kaviraja ('lower than the worm in stool'), and of Mahaprabhu's trinad-api-sunichena verse, which should be strung on the thread of the holy name and worn like a garland around the mind, adding that a devotee's strength is his confidence that the Lord's mercy is greater than his disqualifications—even a fallen soul swept along in the river of time may reach the shore of Goloka. Weaving in Rupa Goswami's prayers (Stava-mala and Padyavali verse 61, the elephant of the mind rescued by the Sudarshana chakra) and the mood of chanting every kirtan as if it were one's last—modeled by Madhava and by a Christian priest who died mid-sermon crying out to his Lord—he closes with Akrura's meditation on descending from his chariot to bow at the lotus feet of Krishna and Balarama and to all the residents of Vraja, longing for the Lord's fragrant lotus hand (scented like the saugandhika lotus of Manasarovara from touching the gopis' faces) to rest upon his head and remove all fear, trusting that Krishna will recognize his devotional heart and not merely a minister of Kamsa.
key_points: Vrindavan is the best place in all of Krishna's creation and Kartika the best time; pilgrims should come as eager students on their 'first day of transcendental school' to learn about Sri Sri Radha-Krishna and serve them with pure devotion (amala-bhakti). Braj-bhasa saying: love is the teacher, Radha and Krishna the students, and the gopis their classmates.

The dham is supremely merciful (an expansion of Lord Balarama, an original spiritual master): even a sinful person who comes automatically chants the names of Krishna and Radha, so Prahlada recommended even his demon father Hiranyakashipu come, and Prabhupada invited the whole world—especially the elderly—to settle permanently and become brajabasis.

Prabhupada lived in Vrindavan not as a kshetra-sannyasi (one who stays in a holy place until death) but treated it as a stop on the way to fulfill his guru's mission in the West, ultimately to bring everyone home to Gokula Vrindavan here or Goloka Vrindavan in the spiritual sky.

Central teaching: one cannot enter Vrindavan simply by purchasing a ticket or being physically present (Krishna Book ch. 38); the ideal process is shown by Akrura, whose footsteps a would-be visitor should follow.

Akrura, sent by Kamsa to bring Krishna and Balarama to Mathura, was a hidden (gupta) devotee who concealed his ecstasy and approached in deep humility, feeling himself a wretched, fallen materialist—so humility is the first qualification for entering Vraj; if one lacks it, one should 'desire to desire' it.

Humility is not imitated but arises from realizing the Lord is great and oneself small—modeled by Prahlada before Nrisimhadev, Krishnadas Kaviraja ('lower than the worm in stool'), and Mahaprabhu's trinad-api-sunichena verse (to be worn like a garland around the mind). A devotee's real strength is trust that the Lord's mercy exceeds his disqualifications.

We are all rupanugas following Prabhupada and Rupa Goswami from shraddha to prema; chant each kirtan as if it were your last (Madhava's mood; the priest who died mid-sermon), longing like Akrura to bow at Krishna and Balarama's lotus feet and all of Vraja, and for the Lord's fragrant lotus hand—scented like the saugandhika lotus of Manasarovara from touching the gopis' faces—to rest on one's head and remove all fear.
references: Krishna Book (Krishna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead), chapter 38 — 'One cannot go to Vrindavan by purchasing a ticket... The process of going to Vrindavan is shown by Akrura'; the thematic core of the lecture.

Srimad-Bhagavatam, Canto 10, chapters 38-39 (Akrura's journey to Vrindavan) — Akrura's humble self-appraisal as a 'wretched materialistic person engaged in sense gratification,' and his meditation on alighting from his chariot to bow at the feet of Krishna and Balarama and all Vraja residents.

Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.38 (Akrura's 'hope against hope' verse) — 'ma evam mamadhamasyapi syad evacyuta-darsanam / hriyamanah kala-nadya kvacit tarati kascana': even a fallen soul swept along in the river of time may sometimes reach the shore and behold the infallible Lord (image of a leaf or stick pushed to the bank).

Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.38 (Akrura's meditation) — 'when I have fallen at His feet, the Almighty Lord will place His lotus hand upon my head; for those who take shelter of Him, disturbed by the serpent of time, that hand removes all fear.'

Srimad-Bhagavatam 4.29.39-40, purport — why Prabhupada loved Vrindavan: 'In a holy place like Vrindavan, if one gets the chance to hear from pure devotees, then the cultivation of Krishna consciousness is very easy.'

Srimad-Bhagavatam 3.20 (purport, Canto 3, ch. 20) — 'any person may go there, and even if he is sinful he will at once contact an atmosphere of spiritual life and automatically chant the names of Krishna and Radha.' (Verse number within the chapter not specified in the talk.)
Srimad-Bhagavatam 4.8.42, purport (Dhruva Maharaj) — unless one is very advanced it is recommended to stay in a holy place such as Prayag, Mathura, or Vrindavan.
Srimad-Bhagavatam 5.13.8, purport — cited by the Swami on becoming elevated to the transcendental world and returning back home, back to Godhead.

Srimad-Bhagavatam, Canto 7 (Prahlada's prayers to Lord Nrisimhadev; approx. 7.9.8-9) — 'How is it possible for me, born in a family of Asuras, to offer suitable prayers... then what is to be said of me?'; 'unless one is very meek and humble it is very difficult to make progress in Krishna consciousness.'

Prabhupada's recommendation (purport, in the context of Prahlada advising Hiranyakashipu) — 'one should go to Vrindavan, where only Krishna consciousness is prevalent... we invite all the elderly persons of the world to come to Vrindavan and stay there in retired life.' (Exact verse citation not stated in the talk.)
Chaitanya-charitamrita — Krishnadas Kaviraja Goswami's humility, 'I am lower/more fallen than the worm in stool' (commonly CC Adi 5.205).

Shikshashtakam, verse 3 (trinad api sunichena taror api sahishnuna...) — humility as the foundation of chanting; the Swami notes Mahaprabhu's instruction (in Chaitanya-charitamrita) to string this verse on the thread of the holy name and wear it like a garland around one's neck/mind for continuous remembrance.

Padyavali (compiled by Rupa Goswami), verse 61 — 'the elephant of my mind is drowning in the waters of material illusion, held by the crocodile of the threefold misery; O Lord Hari, rescue it with Your glowing Sudarshana chakra.'

Stava-mala (Rupa Goswami) — prayer to Vrindavan: 'was there ever anyone who did not quickly attain supreme transcendental bliss by serving you? ... kindly disclose to me the best way to receive the darshan of your worshipable Lord Sri Sri Radha and Krishna.'

Prayer glorifying Rupa Goswami (quoted, source text not named) — 'for the purification of my body I bathe in water; for the complete purification of my existence I bathe in the nectar of the words of Sri Rupa Goswami.'
Vrindavan Days (Hayagriva Dasa) — Prabhupada: 'I lived very simply in Vrindavan, content to be in Rupa Goswami's presence... but I still like Vrindavan best of all.'
Srila Prabhupada-lilamrita (Satsvarupa Dasa Goswami) — Prabhupada in New York: 'my heart is always hankering after that Vrindavan.'
Letter of Srila Prabhupada, 9 November 1975 — 'Anyone who can stay permanently is welcome. I want that as many devotees stay permanently and become brajabasis. This will be very inspiring.'
Hari-bhakti-vilasa — devotees are humble, do not display their japa-mala or proudly announce their guru, keeping their devotion hidden (gupta).
Puranic reference to the saugandhika lotus of Lake Manasarovara — the acharyas say Krishna's lotus hand carries its fragrance, acquired by touching the faces of the gopis.
